slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 14, use 14.2.1 Initializing Pointers with nullptr as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. nullptr represents a null pointer value and communicates absence more clearly than an integer zero used for that purpose. Initialize optional pointers explicitly so that the absence state is defined. A pointer’s nullability belongs in the interface contract: can the caller omit the object, and what does the function do when it is absent? A null pointer does not own an object and must not be dereferenced. A nonnull raw pointer does not automatically own its target either. Keep those two concepts separate. Later smart pointers encode ownership, while optional values encode absence without necessarily using indirection. Choose the representation that matches the domain rather than using pointers for every missing value. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.title: 14.2.2 Checking Pointer Validity Before Dereferencing
keyPoints: An if (pointer != nullptr) check establishes only that the pointer is not null.
It cannot prove that the object is still alive.
Correct pointer use depends on a design that bounds the pointer’s lifetime relative to the owner’s lifetime and.
For a pointer into a local array used within the same block, the relationship is straightforward.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 14, use 14.2.2 Checking Pointer Validity Before Dereferencing as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. An if (pointer != nullptr) check establishes only that the pointer is not null. It cannot prove that the object is still alive. Correct pointer use depends on a design that bounds the pointer’s lifetime relative to the owner’s lifetime and prevents invalidation while access is in progress. For a pointer into a local array used within the same block, the relationship is straightforward. For a pointer stored in a long-lived object or passed between threads, it is not. Document whether a callee retains the pointer, whether a container may reallocate, and whether another thread can destroy the object. Prefer interfaces that make those relationships difficult to violate. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.title: 14.3.1 Moving Between Contiguous Elements
keyPoints: Pointer arithmetic is defined within an array object and its one-past position.
Adding one to a pointer to an element advances by one element, not one byte, according to the pointed-to type.
The one-past pointer is useful as an end sentinel but must not be dereferenced.
Subtracting suitable pointers into the same array gives an element distance.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 14, use 14.3.1 Moving Between Contiguous Elements as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Pointer arithmetic is defined within an array object and its one-past position. Adding one to a pointer to an element advances by one element, not one byte, according to the pointed-to type. The one-past pointer is useful as an end sentinel but must not be dereferenced. Subtracting suitable pointers into the same array gives an element distance. Do not subtract pointers from unrelated allocations and interpret the result as a portable distance. A scalar object has limited array-like treatment for these rules, but that does not make neighboring unrelated objects part of one collection. Standard iterators and spans express many of these boundaries more clearly. slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 14, use Follow the two objects as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Before selection, the pointer has no target. After validation, it observes the second array element. Incrementing the pointed-to value changes the array from three, six, nine to three, seven, nine. The pointer object still identifies that same element. The traversal then uses a beginning pointer and a one-past end pointer. The current pointer visits exactly three live elements and is compared with the excluded end before each dereference. The program neither allocates nor releases memory. Every pointer is a borrowed access path into the local array. slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 14, use Starting exercise: solution notes as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. An index equal to size is outside the element range. A pointer/count function can explicitly permit an empty range, but its implementation must avoid invalid pointer operations and dereferences on that path. A contract should define this rather than relying on caller intuition. A vector append can reallocate its backing storage. A stable record identifier followed by a fresh lookup avoids retaining the invalidated address. An index can also work when ordering and erasure rules preserve its meaning, but it still needs validation before reuse. A nonnull value can still refer to expired, invalidated, out-of-range, or unsuitable storage. Nullness is only one part of validity. Why may an end pointer exist without being dereferenced? It represents the boundary of a permitted half-open range, not an additional element. Why does assigning null not repair every alias? It changes one pointer object. slides.title: Inspecting an Object Address Through a Pointer
keyPoints: Predict the output before running
Use stdout as behavioral evidence
Empty stderr matters because diagnostics have their own channel

slides.narration: This is a chapter listing, not a detached toy. Before running or reading it, state what behavior the program is supposed to witness. Inspecting an Object Address Through a Pointer gives us an executable slice of Chapter 14. The expected stdout is not decorative; it is the behavioral witness for this example. The first visible line is 'value=42 same=true'. If there are multiple lines, read them in order because order often encodes loop progression, branch selection, or state changes. Expected stderr is empty, which means normal behavior is being reported through stdout rather than the diagnostic channel. Expected exit code is 0, so the operating system sees the run as successful after the program finishes printing. If the displayed output ever differs after an edit, do not jump straight to 'wrong.' Ask which requirement changed, which path executed, and whether the difference belongs on stdout, stderr, or the process status.

#include <iostream>
int main(){ int value=42; int* p=&value; std::cout << "value=" << *p << " same=" << std::boolalpha << (p==&value) << '\n'; }

checks.prompt: Explain the output, do not just read it. What does stdout prove here?

Expected stderr is empty, which means normal behavior is being reported through stdout rather than the diagnostic channel. Expected exit code is 0, so the operating system sees the run as successful after the program finishes printing.
